title: Which end do you hit?
objectives: Compute absorption probabilities with first-step analysis.
Write the absorption probabilities as $(I - Q)^{-1}R$ and check one numerically.

screens.title: Where the chance ends up
screens.prose: The fair walk on 0 to 3 again, absorbed at both ends, now starting at 2. Slide $k$ and watch the chance pile up at the two ends.
screens.question: In the long run, what is the chance the walk ends at 3?

options.why: You treated both ends as equally likely. From 2 the walk is next to 3, so 3 is likelier.
That is the chance at the other end, 0. Read node 3 at $k = 12$.
The walk can still wander to 0: at step 2 it is there with chance 0.25.

hints.text: Slide $k$ to 12 and read nodes 0 and 3.

feedback.correct: Two thirds of the walks end at 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $k$ to 12 and read node 3.

explain.text: By step 12 node 3 holds 0.667 and node 0 holds 0.333. Almost nothing is still moving: $(\tfrac12)^{12} \approx 0.0002$. Next we find these numbers exactly.

screens.title: One step, then afresh
screens.prose: Let $h_i$ be the chance of ending at 3, starting from $i$. So $h_3 = 1$ and $h_0 = 0$. From 1 the walk steps to 0 or to 2, each with chance $\tfrac12$, and then starts afresh.
screens.question: Which equation holds for $h_1$?

options.why: You carried the $+1$ over from expected steps. A chance does not grow per step; we only average where the walk lands.
You set $h_0 = 1$. Ending at 0 means not ending at 3, so $h_0 = 0$.
You added the two branches without their chances of $\tfrac12$ each.

hints.text: After one step, where can the walk be?
At 0, with chance $\tfrac12$, or at 2, with chance $\tfrac12$.
Average the chances from those two places: $\tfrac12 h_0 + \tfrac12 h_2$.

feedback.correct: Average over where the first step lands.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight each place the walk can land by its chance.

explain.text: After one step the walk is at 0 or 2, each with chance $\tfrac12$, and starts afresh. So $h_1 = \tfrac12 h_0 + \tfrac12 h_2 = \tfrac12 h_2$. This is first-step analysis without the $+1$, because no steps are being counted.

screens.title: Solve the pair
screens.prose: Use $h_1 = \tfrac12 h_2$, and the same reasoning from 2. Find $h_2$, then $h_1$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $h_2 = \tfrac12 h_1 + \tfrac12$, since $h_3 = 1$: at 3 the walk has ended there
$\tfrac34 h_2 = \tfrac12$, so $h_2 = \tfrac23$, collect the $h_2$ terms and divide

hints.text: Start with the first-step equation from 2.
Then put in the boundary value $h_3 = 1$.
First step, boundary, substitute, solve, back-substitute.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the first-step equation from 2 before using any values.

byKey.a2: The boundary value goes into an equation, so the first-step equation comes first.
byKey.a3: Substituting $h_1$ needs the line with $h_3 = 1$ already used.
byKey.a4: Collecting terms needs the substituted line.
byKey.a5: $h_1$ comes from $h_2$, so it is found last.

explain.text: $h_1 = \tfrac13$ and $h_2 = \tfrac23$, as the slider showed. The chance rises in a straight line from 0 at state 0 to 1 at state 3. For a fair walk it is the distance from the bottom over the width.

screens.title: A walk with a drift
screens.prose: Now the walk on 0 to 3 steps up with chance $\tfrac23$ and down with chance $\tfrac13$. First-step analysis gives $h_1 = \tfrac23 h_2$ and $h_2 = \tfrac13 h_1 + \tfrac23$.
screens.question: Solve the pair and fill in the table, as decimals.

hints.text: Substitute $h_1 = \tfrac23 h_2$ into the second equation.
$h_2 = \tfrac29 h_2 + \tfrac23$.
$\tfrac79 h_2 = \tfrac23$, so $h_2 = \tfrac67$. Then $h_1 = \tfrac23 \times \tfrac67$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Eliminate $h_1$, solve for $h_2$, then back-substitute.

explain.text: $h_2 = \tfrac67 \approx 0.857$ and $h_1 = \tfrac47 \approx 0.571$. The upward drift lifts both above the fair values $\tfrac23$ and $\tfrac13$. Level 3 solves this for any width and drift: gambler's ruin.

screens.title: All at once, as a matrix
screens.prose: A loan is rated A or B each year until it is repaid or defaults. $Q$ holds the chances between A and B, and $R$ the chances into repaid and default. Then $H = (I - Q)^{-1}R$ holds every absorption chance at once.

state.caption: $Q = \begin{pmatrix}0.3 & 0.1\\ 0.2 & 0.4\end{pmatrix}$, and $\det(I - Q) = 0.4$. Rows A, B; columns of $R$: repaid, default.

screens.question: Multiply $(I - Q)^{-1}$ by $R$ and fill in $H$.

hints.text: Row A of $H$ is row A of $(I - Q)^{-1}$ times each column of $R$.
Row B: $0.5 \times 0.5 + 1.75 \times 0.2 = 0.6$. Each row of $H$ adds to 1.

feedback.correct: A loans are repaid 80% of the time, B loans 60%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply row by column, and check that each row of $H$ adds to 1.

byKey.r0c1: Row A times the repaid column: $1.5 \times 0.5 + 0.25 \times 0.2$.
byKey.r1c1: Row B times the repaid column: $0.5 \times 0.5 + 1.75 \times 0.2$.
byKey.r0c2: Row A times the default column: $1.5 \times 0.1 + 0.25 \times 0.2$.
byKey.r1c2: Row B times the default column: $0.5 \times 0.1 + 1.75 \times 0.2$.

explain.text: Each row of $H$ adds to 1: every loan is eventually repaid or defaults. Check row A by first-step analysis: $h_A = 0.5 + 0.3(0.8) + 0.1(0.6) = 0.8$. The matrix formula is the same linear system, solved for both targets at once.

screens.title: Only one way out
screens.prose: A chain with transient states 1, 2, 3 and one absorbing state, X. Every transient state can reach X, though some routes loop back first.

state.caption: X is the only absorbing state.

screens.question: What is $h_1 = P(\text{absorbed at X} \mid \text{start at } 1)$?

options.why: 0.3 is the one-step chance from 2 to X. The chain gets as many tries as it needs.
You multiplied 0.5 by 0.3 along one route. The chain can loop round and try again.
State 1 has no arrow to X, but it reaches X through 2.

hints.text: Where else can the chain end up?
X is the only absorbing state, and every other state can reach it.
So the chain is absorbed at X for sure.

feedback.correct: The chain must end somewhere, and X is the only place.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the places the chain can end up for good.

explain.text: The chain must be absorbed somewhere, and X is the only absorbing state; so $h = 1$ from every state that can reach X. The equations agree: $h_i = 1$ solves $h_i = \sum_j P_{ij} h_j$, since each row adds to 1. Only the time taken depends on the start.

screens.title: Both ends worth 1?
screens.prose: The fair walk on 0 to 4. A colleague sets $h_0 = 1$ and $h_4 = 1$, solves, and gets $h_1 = h_2 = h_3 = 1$. She concludes the walk is sure to reach 4.
screens.question: What is the correct $h_1 = P(\text{reach 4 before 0} \mid \text{start at } 1)$?

options.why: You gave both ends the value 1. Then $h$ is the chance of reaching either end, which is always 1.
You split evenly between the ends. Start 1 sits next to 0, so 0 is likelier.
That is the chance of reaching 0 first, $1 - h_1$.

hints.text: What does $h_0$ mean in words?
Starting at 0, the walk has already ended at 0, not at 4. So $h_0 = 0$.
A fair walk gives a straight line: $h_i = i/4$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $h_0 = 0$ and $h_4 = 1$, then solve.

byKey.both: You set both boundary values to 1. That measures absorbed somewhere, which is certain. Set $h_0 = 0$.

explain.text: With $h_0 = 0$ and $h_4 = 1$, each $h_i$ is the average of its neighbours, so $h$ is a straight line: $(\tfrac14, \tfrac12, \tfrac34)$. Her system answered a different question, absorbed at either end, which is certain. The boundary values decide what $h$ measures.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: For two absorbing states A and B, $$h_i = \sum_j P_{ij}\, h_j, \qquad h_A = 1, \; h_B = 0.$$ There is no $+1$: we average, we do not count steps. The equations are linear in $h$, so $(I - Q)h = r$, where $r$ holds the one-step chances into A.
screens.question: For the fair walk on 0 to 3, what is $P(\text{end at } 0 \mid \text{start at } 1)$?

options.why: That is $h_1$, the chance of ending at 3. Ending at 0 is the other outcome.
You split evenly. Start 1 is next to 0, so 0 is likelier.
The walk reaches 3 first a third of the time.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The walk ends at 0 or at 3, so the two chances add to 1.

explain.text: Swap the boundary values, $g_0 = 1$ and $g_3 = 0$, and the same equations give the chance of ending at 0. Since the walk ends somewhere, $g_i = 1 - h_i$, so $g_1 = \tfrac23$.

screens.title: Will the order fill?
screens.prose: The order queue from the last lesson. At the back an order stays with 0.6, moves to the front with 0.3, or is cancelled with 0.1. At the front it stays with 0.5, fills with 0.4, or is cancelled with 0.1.

state.caption: Each minute. Filled and Cancelled end the order.

screens.question: Fill in the chance each order is filled rather than cancelled.

hints.text: At the front: $h_F = 0.5h_F + 0.4$.
At the back: $h_B = 0.6h_B + 0.3h_F$, since a cancelled order has $h = 0$.

feedback.correct: 80% from the front, 60% from the back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set $h = 1$ at Filled and $h = 0$ at Cancelled, then solve the front first.

explain.text: $h_F = 0.4 / 0.5 = 0.8$ and $h_B = 0.3 \times 0.8 / 0.4 = 0.6$. So 40% of orders that join at the back are cancelled before filling. Level 3 runs the same equations on a long line of states: that is gambler's ruin.

ideas: Let $h_i$ be the chance of absorption at A from $i$. Condition on the first step and average: $h_i = \sum_j P_{ij} h_j$.
The boundary values say what $h$ measures: $h_A = 1$ and $h_B = 0$. Setting both to 1 measures absorbed anywhere, which is certain.
The system is linear: $(I - Q)h = r$. All absorption chances at once are $H = (I - Q)^{-1}R$, whose rows add to 1.
summary.trap: No $+1$ here, and the two boundary values differ: $h_A = 1$ and $h_B = 0$.

quiz.prose: A fair walk on 0 to 4 is absorbed at 0 and 4. It starts at 3.
quiz.question: What is the chance it reaches 4 before 0?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. For a fair walk the chance rises in a straight line from 0 to 1.

byKey.low: $\tfrac14$ is the chance of reaching 0 first.
byKey.half: You split evenly. Start 3 is next to 4.

explain.text: For a fair walk $h_i$ is the average of its neighbours, so $h$ is linear with $h_0 = 0$ and $h_4 = 1$. That gives $h_i = i/4$, and $h_3 = \tfrac34$.

quiz.prose: Each minute, an order at the front stays with chance 0.5, fills with 0.3, or is cancelled with 0.2.
quiz.question: What is the chance it is eventually filled?

byKey.one-minute: 0.3 is the chance of a fill in the first minute. The order gets more minutes.
byKey.plus1: You added 1 as for expected time. A chance has no $+1$.

explain.text: Condition on the first minute: $h = 0.5h + 0.3$. So $h = 0.3 / 0.5 = 0.6$. In words: of the minutes that end the order, 3 in 5 are fills.

quiz.prose: A finite chain has exactly one absorbing state, D, and every other state can reach D.
quiz.question: What is $P(\text{absorbed at D})$ from any state?

options.why: The time taken depends on the start, but D is the only place to end.
$\pi_D = 1$ here, but the reason is simpler: D is the only absorbing state.

options.text: Less than 1, since the chain can loop
options.why: Loops delay absorption but cannot avoid it in a finite chain where every state reaches D.

feedback.correct: Absorption is certain, and D is the only place to be absorbed.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask where else the chain could end up for good.

explain.text: In a finite chain where every state can reach D, the chain is absorbed with chance 1. D is the only absorbing state, so $h = 1$ everywhere. Only the expected time differs from state to state.

quiz.prose: Two transient states with $Q = \begin{pmatrix}0.5 & 0\\ 0 & 0.5\end{pmatrix}$, so $(I - Q)^{-1} = 2I$. Into absorbing states A and B, $R = \begin{pmatrix}0.3 & 0.2\\ 0.1 & 0.4\end{pmatrix}$.
quiz.question: From transient state 2, what is the chance of absorption at A?

widget.label: Chance of absorption at A from state 2

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply row 2 of $2I$ by the A column of $R$.

byKey.raw: 0.1 is the one-step chance from state 2 to A. The chain can wait and try again.
byKey.colB: 0.8 is the chance of absorption at B from state 2.

explain.text: $H = (I - Q)^{-1}R = 2R$, so row 2 is $(0.2, 0.8)$. By first-step analysis, $h_2 = 0.5h_2 + 0.1$ gives 0.2 too. Each row of $H$ adds to 1.
